claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Browne et al., 2005

claims.claim: Each Parhyale embryo develops a variety of specialized appendages along the anterior-posterior axis that differ in size, shape and pattern.
claims.source: Each embryo develops a variety of specialized appendages along the anterior-posterior axis that differ in size, shape and pattern (Martin et al., 2016; Pavlopoulos et al., 2009; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Martin et al., 2016; Pavlopoulos et al., 2009; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008

claims.claim: Parhyale eggs are 500 µm long.
claims.source: Parhyale eggs have good size and optical properties for microscopic live imaging at cellular resolution; the eggshell is transparent and embryos are 500 µm long with low autofluorescence and light scattering.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of measurement in the manuscript

claims.claim: Parhyale eggs have transparent eggshells.
claims.source: Parhyale eggs have good size and optical properties for microscopic live imaging at cellular resolution; the eggshell is transparent and embryos are 500 µm long with low autofluorescence and light scattering.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of observation in the manuscript

claims.claim: Parhyale embryos have low autofluorescence and light scattering.
claims.source: Parhyale eggs have good size and optical properties for microscopic live imaging at cellular resolution; the eggshell is transparent and embryos are 500 µm long with low autofluorescence and light scattering.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of observation in the manuscript

claims.claim: Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy (LSFM) is an ideal technology for studying how cells form tissues and organs in intact developing embryos.
claims.source: LSFM is an ideal technology for studying how cells form tissues and organs in intact developing embryos (Huisken et al., 2004; Keller et al., 2008; Truong et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Huisken et al., 2004; Keller et al., 2008; Truong et al., 2011

claims.claim: LSFM enables biologists to capture fast and dynamic processes at very high spatiotemporal resolution, over long periods of time, and with minimal bleaching and photo-damage.
claims.source: It enables biologists to capture fast and dynamic processes at very high spatiotemporal resolution, over long periods of time, and with minimal bleaching and photo-damage (Combs and Shroff, 2017; Huisken and Stainier, 2009; Khairy and Keller, 2011; Schmied et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Combs and Shroff, 2017; Huisken and Stainier, 2009; Khairy and Keller, 2011; Schmied et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2014

claims.claim: Multi-view LSFM allows samples to be optically sectioned from multiple angles that can be combined computationally to reconstruct the entire specimen with more isotropic resolution.
claims.source: In addition, samples can be optically sectioned from multiple angles (multi-view LSFM) that can be combined computationally to reconstruct the entire specimen with more isotropic resolution (Chhetri et al., 2015; Krzic et al., 2012; Schmid et al., 2013; Swoger et al., 2007; Tomer et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Chhetri et al., 2015; Krzic et al., 2012; Schmid et al., 2013; Swoger et al., 2007; Tomer et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2013

claims.claim: Software solutions exist for registration of acquired views, fusion of raw views into a single output z-stack, and visualization of the raw and fused images.
claims.source: Software solutions exist for registration of acquired views, fusion of raw views (z-stacks) into a single output z-stack, and visualization of the raw and fused images (Chhetri et al., 2015; Ingaramo et al., 2014; Pietzsch et al., 2015; Preibisch et al., 2014; Preibisch et al., 2010; Rubio-Guivernau et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Chhetri et al., 2015; Ingaramo et al., 2014; Pietzsch et al., 2015; Preibisch et al., 2014; Preibisch et al., 2010; Rubio-Guivernau et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016

claims.claim: Automated approaches for cell segmentation and tracking do not yet reach the precision required for unsupervised extraction of cell lineages.
claims.source: Automated approaches for cell segmentation and tracking have also been developed (Amat et al., 2014; Du et al., 2014; Dufour et al., 2017; Faure et al., 2016; Schiegg et al., 2015; Stegmaier et al., 2016; Ulman et al., 2017), however they do not yet reach the precision required for unsupervised extraction of cell lineages.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Amat et al., 2014; Du et al., 2014; Dufour et al., 2017; Faure et al., 2016; Schiegg et al., 2015; Stegmaier et al., 2016; Ulman et al., 2017 and direct statement

claims.claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the leg and wing primordia become progressively subdivided into distinct cell populations along the anterior-posterior (AP) and dorsal-ventral (DV) axes.
claims.source: As revealed by lineage tracing experiments in the leading arthropod model Drosophila melanogaster, the leg and wing primordia become progressively subdivided into distinct cell populations (called compartments when lineage-restricted) along the anterior-posterior (AP) and dorsal-ventral (DV) axes (Dahmann et al., 2011; Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973; Steiner, 1976).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dahmann et al., 2011; Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973; Steiner, 1976

claims.claim: In Drosophila, Dpp signaling controls dorsal cell fate in the leg and growth via cell proliferation in the wing.
claims.source: In Drosophila, Dpp signaling controls dorsal cell fate in the leg and growth via cell proliferation in the wing (Barrio and Milán, 2017; Bosch et al., 2017; Brook and Cohen, 1996; Matsuda and Affolter, 2017; Rogulja and Irvine, 2005; Svendsen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Barrio and Milán, 2017; Bosch et al., 2017; Brook and Cohen, 1996; Matsuda and Affolter, 2017; Rogulja and Irvine, 2005; Svendsen et al., 2015

claims.claim: Oriented cell divisions have been implicated as a general mechanism in shaping the Drosophila wing and other growing organs.
claims.source: Besides regionalization mechanisms, oriented cell divisions have been implicated as a general mechanism in shaping the Drosophila wing and other growing organs (Baena-López et al., 2005; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Baena-López et al., 2005; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013

claims.claim: Transgenic Parhyale embryos with fluorescently labeled nuclei can be imaged routinely for several consecutive days using Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy.
claims.source: We demonstrate here that transgenic embryos with fluorescently labeled nuclei can be imaged routinely for several consecutive days using Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy (LSFM).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of experimental results in the manuscript

claims.claim: A typical 4 to 5 day long LSFM recording of Parhyale embryos was composed of more than 1 million images resulting in >7 TB datasets.
claims.source: A typical 4 to 5 day long recording was composed of more than 1 million images resulting in >7 TB datasets.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of data characteristics in the manuscript

claims.claim: The relatively slow tempo of Parhyale development enabled imaging of each embryo from multiple highly overlapping views with minimal displacement of nuclei between views acquired in each time-point.
claims.source: The relatively slow tempo of Parhyale development enabled imaging of each embryo from multiple highly overlapping views with minimal displacement of nuclei between views acquired in each time-point (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 1A showing multi-view imaging setup

claims.claim: Segment formation and maturation in Parhyale occurred sequentially in anterior-posterior progression.
claims.source: Segment formation and maturation in Parhyale occurred sequentially in AP progression (Figure 1—video 2).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 1—video 2

claims.claim: Appendage morphogenesis in Parhyale involved patterning, growth and differentiation of ectodermal cells organized in an epithelial monolayer that gave rise to the appendage epidermis.
claims.source: Appendage morphogenesis involved patterning, growth and differentiation of ectodermal cells organized in an epithelial monolayer that gave rise to the appendage epidermis.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of observation in the manuscript

claims.claim: Parhyale limbs were specified at about 3.5 days after egg-lay at 25°C.
claims.source: In our LSFM recordings, we were particularly interested in imaging the limbs in the anterior thorax of Parhyale embryos that were specified at about 3.5 days after egg-lay (AEL) at 25˚C.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of timing in the manuscript

claims.claim: Over 4 days following limb specification, Parhyale limb buds bulged out ventrally, elongated along their proximal-distal axis and became progressively segmented until they acquired their definite morphology at around 8 days AEL.
claims.source: Over the next 4 days, limb buds bulged out ventrally, elongated along their PD axis and became progressively segmented until they acquired their definite morphology at around 8 days AEL (Figure 1C–K and Figure 1—video 2).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 1C–K and Figure 1—video 2

claims.claim: During germband formation, the ectoderm contributing to the posterior head and trunk of Parhyale became organized in a stereotyped grid-like pattern with ordered AP rows and DV columns of cells.
claims.source: During germband formation, the ectoderm contributing to the posterior head and the trunk became organized in a stereotyped grid-like pattern with ordered AP rows and DV columns of cells (Figure 2A–A'') (Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Gerberding et al., 2002; Scholtz, 1990; Wolff and Gerberding, 2015).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 2A–A'' and citations to Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Gerberding et al., 2002; Scholtz, 1990; Wolff and Gerberding, 2015

claims.claim: Each row of cells in the Parhyale germband corresponded to one parasegment.
claims.source: Each row of cells corresponded to one parasegment, which is the unit of early metameric organization in Parhyale embryos, like in Drosophila and other arthropods (Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by citations to Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz et al., 1994

claims.claim: Two rounds of longitudinally-oriented cell divisions in each formed parasegmental row, together with the progressive addition of new parasegments at the posterior end, led to Parhyale embryo axial elongation.
claims.source: Two rounds of longitudinally-oriented cell divisions in each formed parasegmental row (Figure 2B–D'), together with the progressive addition of new parasegments at the posterior end, led to embryo axial elongation (Figure 1C–H).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 2B–D' and Figure 1C–H

claims.claim: MaMuT is a hybrid and extension of two existing Fiji plugins: the BigDataViewer visualization engine and the TrackMate annotation engine.
claims.source: This tool was dubbed MaMuT for Massive Multi-view Tracker (Figure 3) and is a hybrid and extension of two existing Fiji plugins: the BigDataViewer visualization engine (Pietzsch et al., 2015) and the TrackMate annotation engine (Tinevez et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by citations to Pietzsch et al., 2015 and Tinevez et al., 2017

claims.claim: MaMuT can be installed through the Fiji updater.
claims.source: MaMuT can be installed through the Fiji updater and is tightly integrated with the other Fiji plugins for LSFM data processing.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about software availability

claims.claim: The source code for MaMuT is available on GitHub.
claims.source: The source code for MaMuT is available on GitHub (Tinevez et al., 2018; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/MaMuT) and detailed tutorials and training datasets can be found at http://imagej.net/MaMuT.
claims.evidence: Direct statement about software availability with citation to Tinevez et al., 2018

claims.claim: In accordance with previous studies in malacostracan crustaceans and other arthropods, each Parhyale thoracic limb consisted of cells from two neighboring parasegments.
claims.source: In accordance with previous studies in malacostracan crustaceans and other arthropods, our reconstructions demonstrated that each Parhyale thoracic limb consisted of cells from two neighboring parasegments (Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz, 1990; Scholtz et al., 1994; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by citations to Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz, 1990; Scholtz et al., 1994; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008

claims.claim: The T2 limb (limb#1) developed from rows b, c and d of the E4 parasegment and from rows a and b of the E5 parasegment.
claims.source: The T2 limb (referred to as limb#1) that we analyzed in-depth (Figure 4A–E) developed from rows b, c and d of the E4 parasegment and from rows a and b of the following E5 parasegment (Figure 4F–J').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4A–E and Figure 4F–J'

claims.claim: Cells that arose from rows c, d and a occupied the entire length of the limb and body wall parts of the T2 segment.
claims.source: Cells that arose from rows c, d and a occupied the entire length of the limb and body wall parts of the T2 segment, while rows b contributed only to the proximal limb and intersegmental territories (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O'

claims.claim: 34 founder cells constituting the limb#1 primordium were fully tracked over 50 hr of development, giving rise to a total of 361 epidermal cells.
claims.source: We fully tracked 34 founder cells constituting the limb#1 primordium over 50 hr of development, giving rise to a total of 361 epidermal cells (Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of tracking results supported by Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 1

claims.claim: The number of differential divisions observed during 50 hr varied dramatically between cells from just 1 DD in the slowest dividing lateral cells to 5 DDs in the fastest dividing central cells.
claims.source: The number of DDs observed during these 50 hr varied dramatically between cells from just 1 DD in the slowest dividing lateral cells of the primordium (cells E4b8, E5a9/b9) to 5 DDs in the fastest dividing central cells (cells E4c3-c6 and E4d3-d6).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of quantitative results from tracking data

claims.claim: The reconstruction of limb#1 is the most comprehensive lineage tree for any developing arthropod limb published to date.
claims.source: Although the clonal composition of crustacean appendages had been described previously with lipophilic dye injections (Wolff and Scholtz, 2008), the reconstruction presented here is the most comprehensive lineage tree for any developing arthropod limb published to date (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement comparing to previous work with citation to Wolff and Scholtz, 2008 and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: During limb specification and outgrowth there was a straight clonal boundary running between the anterior cells derived from the E4b, c and d rows and the posterior cells derived from the E5a and b rows.
claims.source: In agreement with this AP restriction, during limb specification and outgrowth there was a straight clonal boundary running between the anterior cells derived from the E4b, c and d rows and the posterior cells derived from the E5a and b rows (Figure 4F–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4F–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O'

claims.claim: A DV separation took place at the 4-row-parasegment, running between the E4b and c rows anteriorly, between the E5a and b rows posteriorly, and between cells E4c4-c5, E4d3-d4 and E5a4-a5 medially.
claims.source: This analysis suggested that there is indeed a DV separation that took place at the 4-row-parasegment. The DV boundary ran between the E4b and c rows anteriorly, between the E5a and b rows posteriorly, and between cells E4c4-c5, E4d3-d4 and E5a4-a5 medially (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 4F

claims.claim: Throughout limb#1 development, the dorsal and ventral cells formed a sharp boundary between themselves extending along the PD axis.
claims.source: Throughout limb#1 development, the dorsal and ventral cells formed a sharp boundary between themselves extending along the PD axis (Figure 4F–J').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4F–J'

claims.claim: Four identical compartments (anterior-dorsal, anterior-ventral, posterior-dorsal and posterior-ventral) could be derived in limb#2 with straight boundaries and no cell mixing between neighboring compartments.
claims.source: Four identical compartments (anterior-dorsal, anterior-ventral, posterior-dorsal and posterior-ventral) could be derived in this independent reconstruction with straight boundaries and no cell mixing between neighboring compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H'

claims.claim: The second mitotic wave creating the 4-row-parasegment propagated from anterior to posterior rows and from medial to lateral columns.
claims.source: Analysis of the birth sequence of the founder cells in the two reconstructed T2 limbs largely confirmed that the second mitotic wave creating the 4-row-parasegment propagated from anterior to posterior rows and from medial to lateral columns (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—source data 1

claims.claim: Division of the posterior cd cells within the 2-row-parasegment was slightly more advanced temporally compared to their anterior ab sister cells.
claims.source: First, as previously noted (Scholtz, 1990), division of the posterior cd cells within the 2-row-parasegment was slightly more advanced temporally compared to their anterior ab sister cells (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5A–C and citation to Scholtz, 1990

claims.claim: The temporal sequence of divisions exhibited a certain degree of variability between the two analyzed limbs.
claims.source: Second, the temporal sequence of divisions, which gave rise to a stereotyped number and spatial arrangement of the 34 founder cells in each primordium, exhibited a certain degree of variability between the two analyzed limbs; for example, division of the E4cd8/9 cells preceded division of E4cd7 in limb#1 but not in lim#2, whereas division of the E4cd6/7 cells preceded division of E4cd5 in limb#2 but not in limb#1 (Figure 5A–B).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of comparative analysis supported by Figure 5A–B

claims.claim: It was possible to register the two growth curves during the period when all cells were tracked faithfully by applying a linear temporal rescaling factor of 1.6.
claims.source: Yet, it was possible to register the two growth curves during the period when all cells were tracked faithfully by applying a linear temporal rescaling factor of 1.6, effectively correcting for the temperature-induced change in growth (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of analysis method supported by Figure 5D

claims.claim: After temporal alignment, the increase in cell number was very similar between developing limbs, up to 35 hr after the first tracked division.
claims.source: After this temporal alignment, the increase in cell number was very similar between developing limbs, up to 35 hr after the first tracked division.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of analysis results

claims.claim: The first step in limb bud formation was the rise of few cells at the intersection of the four compartments above the level of the germband at around 96 hr AEL.
claims.source: At the cellular level, the first step in this transformation was the rise of few cells at the intersection of the four compartments above the level of the germband at around 96 hr AEL (Figure 4G,G' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,F').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4G,G' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,F'

claims.claim: Within 3 hr following the initial rise of cells, this initial phase was followed by a large-scale elevation of most cells in the dorsal compartment.
claims.source: Within the following 3 hr, this initial phase was followed by a large-scale elevation of most cells in the dorsal compartment.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of observation

claims.claim: The intersection of the AP and DV boundaries was at the tip of the limb bud and persisted in this position throughout subsequent elongation.
claims.source: The intersection of the AP and DV boundaries was at the tip of the limb bud and persisted in this position throughout subsequent elongation (Figure 4H–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–H').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4H–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–H'

claims.claim: From 103 hr AEL onwards, a second element appeared bulging distally off the original bud in limb#1.
claims.source: From 103 hr AEL onwards, a second element appeared bulging distally off the original bud in limb#1 (Figure 4I,I').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4I,I'

claims.claim: The limb elongated as a convoluted rather than straight cylinder and acquired progressively an S-shape.
claims.source: The limb elongated as a convoluted rather than straight cylinder and acquired progressively an S-shape (Figure 4J,J').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4J,J'

claims.claim: There was a striking difference in cell cycle length between central cells that were dividing faster than their neighbors in the periphery of the primordium (average CCL 7.1–8.5 hr versus 8.5–16.4 hr, respectively).
claims.source: This quantification revealed a striking difference in CCL between central cells that were dividing faster than their neighbors in the periphery of the primordium (average CCL 7.1–8.5 hr versus 8.5–16.4 hr, respectively).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of quantitative analysis results

claims.claim: The difference in cell cycle length started from early primordium specification at the 4-row-parasegment.
claims.source: This difference started from early primordium specification at the 4-row-parasegment (Figure 6E), but became most pronounced during the global elevation of the limb bud (Figure 4F), suggesting a causal association between spatially controlled cell proliferation and initiation of limb outgrowth (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6E and Figure 4F

claims.claim: During subsequent elongation stages, a high concentration of fast dividing cells was located at the intersection of the four presumptive compartments, resembling a growth zone at the distal tip of the growing appendage.
claims.source: During subsequent elongation stages, a high concentration of fast dividing cells was located at the intersection of the four presumptive compartments, resembling a growth zone at the distal tip of the growing appendage (Figure 6G,H).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6G,H

claims.claim: Another row of faster dividing cells was localized in the anterior cells abutting the AP boundary.
claims.source: Another row of faster dividing cells was localized in the anterior cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 6H,H').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6H,H'

claims.claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed that the 34 founder cells formed three clusters based on their division patterns.
claims.source: This analysis revealed very similar profiles in the two limbs, as well as their average, with their cells forming three clusters (Figure 7A–C and Figure 7—source data 1): the first cluster contained cells E4c3-c7 and E4d3-d7 displaying the fastest proliferation rates and giving rise to most of the limb structures; the second cluster contained the majority of E4 and E5 b cells corresponding to the slowest dividing cells of ventral fate and contributing to the proximal limb and intersegmental territories; the third cluster contained the remaining cells exhibiting mixed division patterns, including most of the posterior E5a cells and the more lateral E4c and d cells.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of clustering analysis results supported by Figure 7A–C and Figure 7—source data 1

claims.claim: Pairwise comparisons revealed low distances between the 34 homologous cells in limb#1 and limb#2 with a median difference of 19.3%.
claims.source: Pairwise comparisons revealed low distances between the 34 homologous cells in limb#1 and limb#2 with a median difference of 19.3% (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of quantitative comparison supported by Figure 7D

claims.claim: The distribution of distances between homologous cells was significantly shifted towards lower values relative to pairwise comparisons between non-homologous cells across the two limbs.
claims.source: The distribution of these distances between homologous cells was significantly shifted towards lower values relative to pairwise comparisons between non-homologous cells across the two limbs (Figure 7D and Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison supported by Figure 7D and Figure 7—source data 1

claims.claim: All early divisions in the limb#1 primordium were parallel to the AP axis confirming the strict longitudinal orientation of row divisions.
claims.source: All early divisions in the limb#1 primordium were parallel to the AP axis confirming the strict longitudinal orientation of row divisions (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 8F

claims.claim: Cell divisions acquired a more heterogeneous pattern after the 4-row-parasegment.
claims.source: Cell divisions acquired a more heterogeneous pattern after the 4-row-parasegment (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 8G

claims.claim: An increasing number of mitotic spindles aligned progressively along the PD axis during limb bud formation and elongation.
claims.source: An increasing number of mitotic spindles aligned progressively along the PD axis during limb bud formation (Figure 8H) and elongation (Figure 8I,J).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 8H, Figure 8I, and Figure 8J

claims.claim: Parhyale limb outgrowth is driven by at least two patterned cell behaviors: the differential rates of cell proliferation and the orderly arrangement of mitotic spindles.
claims.source: Collectively, the information extracted from our spatiotemporally resolved lineage trees strongly suggested that Parhyale limb outgrowth is driven by at least two patterned cell behaviors: the differential rates of cell proliferation and the orderly arrangement of mitotic spindles.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of inference from data analysis

claims.claim: The cells that gave rise to the proximal, medial and distal limb segments occupied distinct mediolateral positions in the germband grid at the 4-row-parasegment and distinct PD positions in the early limb bud.
claims.source: This analysis showed that the cells that gave rise to the proximal, medial and distal limb segments occupied distinct mediolateral positions in the germband grid at the 4-row-parasegment (Figure 9M) and distinct PD positions in the early limb bud (Figure 9N).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9M and Figure 9N

claims.claim: When the limb bud split into two elements, the proximal element gave rise to the proximal limb segments coxa, basis and ischium, while the distal element gave rise to the distal limb segments merus, carpus, propodus, and dactylus.
claims.source: When the limb bud split into two elements, the proximal element gave rise to the proximal limb segments coxa, basis and ischium, while the distal element gave rise to the distal limb segments merus, carpus, propodus, and dactylus (Figure 9O–R).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9O–R

claims.claim: The cells forming the distal segments originated as a disc of cells centered at the intersection of the four compartments with contributions from the E4c4-c6, E4d3-d6 and E5a3-a6 sublineages.
claims.source: The cells forming the distal segments originated as a disc of cells centered at the intersection of the four compartments with contributions from the E4c4-c6, E4d3-d6 and E5a3-a6 sublineages (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: During the subsequent elongation stages, distal cells kept separate from more proximal cells at the prospective ischium/merus joint.
claims.source: During the subsequent elongation stages, distal cells kept separate from more proximal cells at the prospective ischium/merus joint, suggesting that limb segments may pose secondary lineage restrictions along the PD axis (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) (Milán and Cohen, 2000).
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and citation to Milán and Cohen, 2000

claims.claim: The region of high/moderate Ph-dpp expression was localized to rows E4c, E4d and E5a that mostly contribute to the presumptive dorsal compartment.
claims.source: Acknowledging that the graded Ph-dpp expression obscured the precise limits of its expression, this analysis suggested that the region of high/moderate Ph-dpp expression was localized to rows E4c, E4d and E5a that mostly contribute to the presumptive dorsal compartment, while low/no Ph-dpp expression could be detected in the prospective ventral rows E4b anteriorly and E5b posteriorly (Figure 10A'').
claims.evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 10A''

claims.claim: Ph-dpp expression faded in the medial (prospective ventral) columns and the border between high/moderate and low/no expressing cells was located in descendent cells from column 4.
claims.source: Furthermore, Ph-dpp expression faded in the medial (prospective ventral) columns and the border between high/moderate and low/no expressing cells was located in descendent cells from column 4 as also predicted by our in silico cellular analysis (Figure 10A–A'').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10A–A''

claims.claim: In embryos 96–108 hr AEL, the domain of strong Ph-dpp expression was more localized in the row of anterior-dorsal cells abutting the AP boundary.
claims.source: In embryos 96–108 hr AEL, the domain of strong Ph-dpp expression was more localized in the row of anterior-dorsal cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 10D–D'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1D,D').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10D–D'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1D,D'

claims.claim: Expression of Ph-Doc was detected in a subset of the Ph-dpp-expressing cells at 84–96 hr AEL.
claims.source: Expression of the single Doc gene identified in Parhyale (Ph-Doc) was detected in a subset of the Ph-dpp-expressing cells at 84–96 hr AEL (Figure 10B–B'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B,B'), while 12 hr later the two genes exhibited essentially identical strong expression in the cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 10E–E'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,E').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10B–B'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B,B'

claims.claim: 12 hr after 84-96 hr AEL, Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc exhibited essentially identical strong expression in the cells abutting the AP boundary.
claims.source: Expression of the single Doc gene identified in Parhyale (Ph-Doc) was detected in a subset of the Ph-dpp-expressing cells at 84–96 hr AEL (Figure 10B–B'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B,B'), while 12 hr later the two genes exhibited essentially identical strong expression in the cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 10E–E'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,E').
claims.evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10E–E'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,E'

claims.claim: Cells expressing Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc exhibited the highest rates of cell proliferation.
claims.source: In both stages analyzed, cells expressing Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc also exhibited the highest rates of cell proliferation (compare Figure 10D'',E'' with Figure 6G,H) providing strong correlative evidence for a morphogen-dependent control of Parhyale limb growth.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of correlation supported by comparison of Figure 10D'',E'' with Figure 6G,H

claims.claim: Ph-H15 transcripts were detected specifically in the b row cells.
claims.source: In agreement with these predictions, in situ hybridization analyses detected the Ph-H15 transcripts specifically in the b row cells.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of in situ hybridization results

results.result: The authors successfully established multi-view LSFM imaging protocols for Parhyale embryos, enabling long-term imaging at cellular resolution. Transgenic embryos with H2B-mRFPruby-labeled nuclei were imaged for 4-5 days, generating >7 TB datasets with >1 million images, using optimized parameters including 7.5 min intervals, periodic heat-shock for fluorescence replenishment, and multi-view acquisition.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 and C72-C78 provide comprehensive methodological details and demonstrate successful long-term imaging. The imaging parameters are well-documented (C73, C75, C76), quality control was performed (C78), and the resulting data characteristics are quantified (C15, C83). The slow developmental tempo of Parhyale (C16) enabled the multi-view approach with minimal nuclear displacement between views.

results.result: The authors developed MaMuT (Massive Multi-view Tracker), a novel software tool for manual cell tracking in large multi-dimensional datasets. MaMuT integrates BigDataViewer and TrackMate, enables synergistic annotation from multiple views, and was used to reconstruct the complete T2 limb lineage requiring ~10 weeks of manual tracking by an expert annotator.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 and C84-C86 establish MaMuT's technical foundation and capabilities. The software is openly available (C25, C26), handles up to ~100,000 annotations efficiently (C117), and enabled comprehensive lineage reconstruction (C86). The time investment (C71, C114) and advantages of manual tracking (C115, C116) are clearly documented. The unique multi-view annotation capability (C85) is a key innovation.

results.result: Complete single-cell lineage reconstruction of the Parhyale T2 limb (limb#1) was achieved by tracking 34 founder cells over 50 hours, generating 361 epidermal cells. The limb developed from rows b, c, d of E4 parasegment and rows a, b of E5 parasegment, with dramatic variation in division rates (1-5 differential divisions). This represents the most comprehensive lineage tree for any developing arthropod limb to date.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 provide detailed quantitative lineage data with clear spatial and temporal resolution. The parasegmental origin (C27, C28), spatial distribution (C29), complete tracking statistics (C30, C31), and comparison to prior work (C32) are well-documented. The claim of being the most comprehensive arthropod limb lineage (C32) is supported by comparison to previous dye injection studies.

results.result: Digital clonal analysis revealed early lineage restrictions in the developing Parhyale limb along both AP and DV axes. A straight AP boundary separated anterior (E4b,c,d) from posterior (E5a,b) cells throughout development. A DV boundary was identified at the 4-row-parasegment stage, running between E4b/c rows anteriorly, E5a/b rows posteriorly, and through specific medial cells. These boundaries formed four compartments (AD, AV, PD, PV) with no cell mixing, confirmed in an independent limb#2 reconstruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 demonstrate lineage restrictions through comprehensive cell tracking data. The AP boundary (C33) is consistent with known parasegmental organization. The DV boundary (C34, C35) is a novel finding supported by detailed spatial mapping and confirmed in an independent reconstruction (C36). The in silico approach (C87) provides insights not previously accessible in species lacking genetic lineage tracing tools.

results.result: Analysis of founder cell birth sequences confirmed that the second mitotic wave creating the 4-row-parasegment propagated from anterior to posterior rows and medial to lateral columns, with some variability between limbs. Despite imaging at different temperatures (26°C vs 29-30°C), the two limbs showed similar growth patterns after temporal rescaling by a factor of 1.6, with highly reproducible cell numbers up to 35 hours after the first tracked division.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 provide quantitative temporal analysis of cell division patterns. The general anterior-to-posterior, medial-to-lateral progression (C37) is confirmed with noted deviations (C38, C39). The temporal rescaling approach (C40) successfully aligned growth curves from different temperatures, demonstrating reproducibility (C41). The variability noted (C39) is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Limb bud formation involved remodeling of flat epithelium into a 3D bulge through a stereotyped sequence: initial rise of cells at the four-compartment intersection (~96h AEL), followed by large-scale elevation of dorsal compartment cells within 3 hours. The AP/DV boundary intersection marked the limb tip throughout elongation. The limb elongated as a convoluted S-shaped cylinder rather than a straight structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 and C88 describe the morphogenetic process with clear temporal and spatial resolution. The initial cellular events (C42, C43), boundary dynamics (C44), and morphological progression (C45, C46) are documented with specific timepoints and supported by figure references. The 3D epithelial remodeling (C88) is directly observed through the imaging data.

results.result: Quantitative analysis revealed striking spatial patterns in cell proliferation rates. Central cells divided faster than peripheral cells (average CCL 7.1-8.5 hr vs 8.5-16.4 hr), starting from the 4-row-parasegment stage. During elongation, fast-dividing cells concentrated at the distal tip (resembling a growth zone) and along the anterior AP boundary. Hierarchical clustering identified three distinct cell groups based on division patterns, with homologous cells between limb#1 and limb#2 showing significantly more similar division patterns (median 19.3% difference) than non-homologous cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 provide rigorous quantitative analysis of cell proliferation with specific measurements and statistical comparisons. The spatial patterns (C47-C50) are clearly defined with quantitative CCL values. The clustering analysis (C51) and pairwise comparisons (C52, C53) demonstrate reproducibility between limbs with appropriate statistical testing. The association between differential proliferation and limb outgrowth (C48) is appropriately presented as suggestive rather than causal.

results.result: Analysis of mitotic spindle orientations revealed temporal changes in division patterns. Early divisions were strictly longitudinal (parallel to AP axis), but became more heterogeneous after the 4-row-parasegment. During limb bud formation and elongation, an increasing number of mitotic spindles aligned along the proximal-distal axis. These findings suggest that Parhyale limb outgrowth is driven by at least two patterned cell behaviors: differential proliferation rates and orderly spindle arrangement.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 document division orientation patterns with clear temporal progression. The strict early longitudinal orientation (C54), subsequent heterogeneity (C55), and progressive PD alignment (C56) are quantified with rose diagrams showing percentages. The conclusion (C57) appropriately integrates proliferation and orientation data, though it is presented as a suggestion rather than definitive proof of causation.

results.result: Cell fate mapping along the proximal-distal axis showed that cells giving rise to proximal, medial, and distal limb segments occupied distinct positions in the germband grid at the 4-row-parasegment and in the early limb bud. When the limb split into two elements, the proximal element formed coxa, basis, and ischium, while the distal element formed merus, carpus, propodus, and dactylus. Distal segments originated from a disc of cells centered at the four-compartment intersection (E4c4-c6, E4d3-d6, E5a3-a6), and distal cells remained separate from proximal cells at the ischium/merus joint, suggesting secondary lineage restrictions along the PD axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 provide detailed spatial mapping of segment origins with specific cell identities. The distinct positional origins (C58), element-to-segment relationships (C59), and cellular composition of distal segments (C60) are clearly documented. The suggestion of secondary lineage restrictions (C61) is appropriately tentative and supported by citation to similar findings in Drosophila.

results.result: Gene expression analysis validated cellular models of limb patterning. Ph-dpp expression localized to presumptive dorsal rows (E4c, E4d, E5a) at 84-96h AEL, with expression fading in medial columns and the border at column 4 descendants. By 96-108h AEL, strong Ph-dpp expression concentrated in anterior-dorsal cells abutting the AP boundary. Ph-Doc was detected in a subset of Ph-dpp-expressing cells initially, then co-localized with Ph-dpp at the AP boundary. Cells expressing Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc exhibited the highest proliferation rates, providing correlative evidence for morphogen-dependent growth control.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 integrate gene expression with cellular lineage data. The spatial localization of Ph-dpp (C62, C63, C64) and Ph-Doc (C65, C66) is mapped onto reconstructed cell identities with cellular resolution. The correlation with proliferation rates (C67) is appropriately presented as correlative rather than causal. The graded expression and boundary limitations are acknowledged (C62).

results.result: Ph-H15 expression validated the predicted DV compartment boundary. Ph-H15 transcripts were detected specifically in b row cells, with expression initiating shortly after ab cells divided into a and b daughters at the 4-row-parasegment. Although initially activated in all b cells, Ph-H15 expression later faded in medial columns and persisted only in ventral limb cells near the body wall.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 demonstrate precise spatial and temporal correlation between Ph-H15 expression and the predicted ventral cell identity. The b-row specificity (C68), timing relative to cell division (C69), and dynamic expression pattern (C70) all match predictions from the lineage analysis. This provides independent validation of the DV boundary model.

results.result: The Parhyale limb conforms to Meinhardt's boundary model, where a secondary developmental field (the PD axis) initiates and is patterned around the intersection of AP and DV compartment boundaries. The intersection of these boundaries was located at the limb tip and persisted in this position throughout elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C90, and C44 connect the observed cellular organization to an established theoretical framework. The persistent localization of the AP/DV boundary intersection at the limb tip (C44) directly supports the boundary model (C90). However, the claim that Parhyale "perfectly" conforms (C89) may be overstated given that only morphological/positional evidence is provided without functional validation.

results.result: The findings implicate growth-based morphogenesis as a driving mechanism for arthropod limb evagination. Differential cell proliferation between central (faster) and peripheral (slower) regions of the limb primordium, starting from early specification and becoming pronounced during limb bud elevation, suggests a causal association with limb outgrowth. This mechanism has been the dominant hypothesis for vertebrate limb outgrowth for 50 years but has never been implicated in arthropod limb evagination, though pharmacological inhibition of proliferation can reduce limb bud formation in Artemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 establish the historical context, and C48 provides correlative evidence for the association between differential proliferation and limb outgrowth. However, the causal relationship is only suggested, not demonstrated. No functional experiments (e.g., proliferation inhibition in Parhyale) are presented to test causality. The Artemia example (C93) supports plausibility but is from a different species. Claim C94 appropriately characterizes this as demonstrating "functionally interdependent mechanisms" rather than proving causation.

results.result: Analysis of dpp, Doc, and H15 expression in Parhyale suggests conserved roles for these genes in dorsal and ventral cell fate specification, providing independent support for a compartment-based mechanism to pattern the DV axis of arthropod limbs. In Drosophila, Dpp and Wg ligands are induced at the AP boundary in dorsal and ventral cells respectively, creating concentration gradients that pattern the PD axis through limb gap genes and control DV cell fate through T-box selector genes. The PD expression of limb gap genes is conserved in arthropods including Parhyale.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 establish the Drosophila paradigm with appropriate citations. Claim C99 appropriately presents the Parhyale findings as "suggesting" conservation rather than proving it. The gene expression patterns are consistent with conserved roles, and the compartment-based mechanism is supported by both lineage and expression data. However, functional validation would be needed to definitively establish conservation of gene function.

results.result: The authors anticipate that LSFM imaging and tracking approaches, combined with CRISPR/Cas-based genome editing, will provide tools to explore how morphogens regulate growth and form at cellular resolution. The stereotyped organization of Parhyale ectoderm will enable comparison of lineages, cell behaviors, and genes between serially homologous structures within and across embryos and malacostracan crustaceans.
results.evaluation: Claims C100 and C102 present reasonable future directions based on the established methods and biological features of Parhyale. The integration of LSFM/tracking with CRISPR/Cas (C100, citing Kao et al., 2016) is technically feasible. The stereotyped organization enabling comparative studies (C102) is well-supported by the current data and extensive citations. These are appropriately framed as anticipated future applications rather than current results.

results.result: Parhyale hawaiensis is a direct-developing crustacean with favorable biological and optical properties for developmental imaging studies. The body plan is specified during 10 days of embryogenesis, each embryo develops diverse specialized appendages along the AP axis, and eggs are 500 µm long with transparent eggshells, low autofluorescence, and low light scattering. The tempo and mode of development has important ramifications for imaging and tracking.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 establish the biological rationale for using Parhyale, supported by appropriate citations (C1, C2) and direct measurements (C3-C5). These properties are well-documented in the literature and confirmed by the successful imaging results. Claim C101 appropriately connects these properties to the technical feasibility of the approach.

results.result: Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy (LSFM) is an ideal technology for studying tissue and organ formation in intact embryos, enabling capture of fast dynamic processes at high spatiotemporal resolution over long periods with minimal photobleaching and damage. Multi-view LSFM allows computational reconstruction with isotropic resolution. Software solutions exist for registration, fusion, and visualization, but automated cell segmentation and tracking do not yet reach the precision required for unsupervised lineage extraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C10 provide appropriate background on LSFM technology and computational tools, all supported by extensive citations to the relevant literature. The limitation of automated tracking (C10) is well-documented in the cited literature and motivates the development of MaMuT. These claims establish the technical context for the study.

results.result: The authors establish the comparative context for arthropod limb development, contrasting Drosophila with other arthropods including Parhyale. In Drosophila, limb development occurs across embryonic, larval, and pupal stages in flat imaginal discs, with AP compartmentalization during embryogenesis and DV during larval development. In most other arthropods including Parhyale, all limb developmental processes occur during embryogenesis in 3D epithelial outgrowths. The AP boundary is conserved across arthropods at parasegment interfaces, but the DV separation mechanism, timing, and position have remained unexplored at the cellular level due to lack of lineage tracing methodologies.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C103-C110 provide comprehensive comparative context supported by extensive literature citations. The distinctions between Drosophila and other arthropods (C103-C105) are well-established. The conservation of AP boundaries (C107, C108) and uncertainty about DV separation (C109, C110) appropriately frame the knowledge gap addressed by this study. The citations support all factual claims about prior work.

results.result: The authors document the overall developmental progression of Parhyale embryogenesis captured by LSFM. Segment formation occurred sequentially in AP progression. Appendage morphogenesis involved patterning, growth, and differentiation of ectodermal epithelial cells. Limbs were specified at ~3.5 days AEL and acquired definite morphology by ~8 days AEL through ventral bulging, PD elongation, and progressive segmentation. During germband formation, the ectoderm organized into a stereotyped grid with ordered AP rows (parasegments) and DV columns, with two rounds of longitudinal divisions and posterior addition of parasegments driving axial elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23 describe the overall developmental progression with appropriate temporal landmarks and are supported by figure references and citations to prior work. These observations are consistent with established knowledge of Parhyale development and provide context for the detailed lineage analysis. The grid-like organization (C21) and parasegmental structure (C22) are well-documented in the cited literature.

results.result: A second T2 limb (limb#2) was imaged on a different LSFM system at 29-30°C and tracked using SIMI°BioCell software from a single view. The reconstruction was complete up to ~22 hours of imaging time (35 hours when scaled to limb#1 growth rate), after which increasing cell density and signal deterioration made tracking intractable, particularly for medial column descendants.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 document the methods and limitations for the second limb reconstruction. The different imaging conditions (C79), tracking software (C80), completeness (C81), and limitations (C82) are clearly stated. This independent reconstruction provided validation for the limb#1 findings despite being less complete. The limitations are appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: The authors conclude that reconstruction of cell lineages and behaviors provides solid predictions and powerful contexts to study gene expression and function. By combining light-sheet microscopy with new tracking software, they revealed cellular architecture and dynamics underlying epithelial remodeling and organ morphogenesis in a non-conventional model. Expression of Distal-less, an early limb specification marker, is first detected at the 4-row-parasegment in cells at the AP/DV boundary intersection.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 provide appropriate summary statements. The Distal-less expression pattern (C111) is supported by citations and consistent with the boundary model. The conclusions about the value of lineage reconstruction (C112) and the achievement of the study (C113) are justified by the comprehensive data presented. These represent appropriate synthesis of the findings.
